prompt: Explain the Senate filibuster using only baseball rain-delay metaphors. Do not stop when the metaphor stops working.
response:
In this ballpark, the Senate is playing a nine-inning game where the scoreboard can’t change unless the grounds crew officially puts the ball back in play.

A filibuster is when one team decides it doesn’t need to win the inning; it just needs to make sure the tarp never comes off the field.

A senator who filibusters is a player who walks to home plate during a rain delay, refuses to leave the batter’s box, and starts reciting the entire stadium media guide out loud—not to score runs, but to keep everyone from taking the field.

At first, it’s just “We’re waiting out the weather.” Then it becomes “We are now *creating* weather.”

The bill is the game. Majority support is having more fans in your section. None of that matters if the umpires won’t call “Play ball” because one guy keeps insisting the drizzle is “unsafe conditions” and keeps producing new radar maps from his sock.

The traditional “talking filibuster” is a rain delay where the player has to stay at the microphone the whole time, no bathroom breaks, no sitting down, no sunflower seeds—if he stops talking, the grounds crew sprints out, rips off the tarp, and the next pitch gets thrown. So he keeps describing every raindrop individually, giving each one a batting stance and a hometown.

The modern filibuster is a rain delay where the player doesn’t even have to be on the field. He just phones the clubhouse and says, “I object: tarp stays,” and the entire stadium nods solemnly and keeps selling ponchos. The silence itself counts as precipitation.

A “hold” is when a single player quietly slips the umpire a sticky note that says, “I have a strong feeling it might rain later,” and the umpires react like a hurricane siren just went off.
